coach_says: Taking with the queen walks it into a trap: after Bg5 your queen on f6 has no safe square (e7 and d8 are covered by the bishop, f5 and g6 by Bd3, h4 and e5 by the knight), so you lose it for a piece. Before recapturing with the queen, check where it can go if it is attacked. Here gxf6 was the only way to win the piece back; it loosens your king, but you keep material.

Be3 puts a second piece where a black pawn can reach it. After ...d5 your bishop on c4 has to move, and then ...d4 forks the bishop on e3 and the knight on c3, winning a piece. When your pieces sit on the third and fourth ranks in front of an enemy centre pawn, ask what happens if it advances twice. Moving the bishop out of the way first with Ba2, or castling, kept everything safe.
also: pieces in front of enemy pawns

coach_says: a4 lets Black play ...b3 with tempo on your queen, and that pawn on b3 is now a protected passed pawn backed by c4. Worse, your a-pawn no longer guards b4, so the knight jumps to b4 heading for c2 or d3 with check, forking your king and rook. When your opponent's pawns are pressing on your queenside, keep your own pawns where they guard the key squares; Qd1 got the queen off the c2 square before ...b3 could hit it.

You are a pawn down, and your real chance is Black's open king, so you want to keep the queens on. After Qf4 Black answers ...Qe5, and you cannot avoid the queen trade, which leaves you in an endgame a pawn down with a weak d5 pawn. Rc1 was better: it brings your idle rook into the game on the open c-file against c7, and if ...Qe5 your queen can step aside and keep the attack.
concept: allowed a queen trade a pawn down

coach_says: Your b2 pawn was loose: the g7 bishop can take it with tempo on the a1 rook. Ng5 makes that worse, because the knight on e4 was the piece covering c3 and d2, so after ...Bxb2 Rab1 the bishop comes to c3 and attacks your e1 rook too. Ng5 itself threatens nothing, since e6 and f7 are well covered. Bxc7 was the move: take a pawn of your own while hitting the rook on d8, so the b2 pawn is paid for.

You are two pawns down, so you need to make Black's position worse, not make a quiet move like g3. Bxa6 takes the knight on the rim before it reaches c5, where it would hit your bishop and head for e4, and after ...bxa6 Black is left with doubled, isolated a-pawns and a weak c6 pawn you can attack with c4 and your rooks. When you are behind in material, look for trades that damage your opponent's pawns.

In this French-style structure your counterplay comes from hitting White's pawn chain with ...c5. b6 is slow: White simply plays cxd5 cxd5, your c-pawn is gone, and you have no lever against d4 while White grabs space with f4. Play ...dxc4 and ...c5 (or ...c5 at once) straight away, before White can lock the centre.
concept: strike the pawn chain with c5

coach_says: The d4 pawn is attacked twice, by your knight and your queen down the open d-file, and only the f3 knight and the queen defend it. ...g4 kicks that knight away, so White either loses d4 or has to trade queens and stay a pawn down. Bxc3 does the opposite: it gives up your good bishop and, after bxc3, the c3 pawn props up d4 and White gets a strong centre against your king, still in the middle. When a pawn is defended by a piece, look for a way to chase that defender.
also: bishop pair given up for nothing

coach_says: Your queen on g4 is on the same diagonal as Black's c8 bishop, with only the e6 pawn in between, so ...e5 attacks your queen and gains a tempo. Castling long ignores that, and it also takes your king away from f2, which the queen on f6 now hits. Move the queen off the diagonal first (Qh3 or Qg3), and think twice before castling to a queenside where b3 has already loosened the squares around the king.

In a gambit you are two pawns down, so every move has to keep Black busy. Ng5 looks aggressive but threatens nothing (Nxf7 Kxf7 just loses a piece for a pawn), and Black calmly plays ...d6, which stops your e5 push for good. e5 was the move: it kicks the f6 knight, cramps Black and gives your knight e4 and d6.
concept: push e5 to keep the initiative

coach_says: Your king is on h1 with the h-file open and two black rooks ready to use it, so moving your queen to a4 leaves it badly short of defenders. Black answers ...Bxh3, and after gxh3 Rxh3+ the rooks and queen pour in. Before going after the a5 bishop or a7, ask what your opponent is aiming at your king. Bg4 was best: it trades off the e6 bishop that eyes h3.
concept: Bxh3 sacrifice on the open h-file

coach_says: Good move. The rook on g5 attacked your queen, and Qe2 steps away to a safe square where it still helps in the centre. Just be careful not to play Nb5 in these spots: ...Rxg4 wins the queen.
Taking on c3 is fine: you win the pawn back after Qc2 Ne4 Bxe4 dxe4 Qxe4 and stay about level. Developing with ...Bf5 or ...Re8 was a touch more natural, but there is nothing to fix here.
Bd3 is a reasonable developing move, about as good as Be2 here. Black can hit the centre with ...e5 and ...exd4, so be ready to recapture with the knight and keep your pieces active.
Nd5 is fine; it leads to some trades but you stay level. Castling first was a little more solid, since your king is still in the centre with your bishop already committed to h4.

e6 is playable, but it shuts your light-squared bishop in behind your pawns and invites e4, reaching a French-type position. Against this setup it is a little more comfortable to play ...Nf6 and get the c8 bishop out to f5 before ...e6.
The position was already very difficult, and Bxd2 is about as good as the alternatives Kxd2 and Nxd2. The real damage was done earlier in the game.
Rg5 is the engine's top choice: it hits the queen and swings the rook toward White's king. Nothing to change here.
Rd2+ is a good move: it gets a rook to the second rank with check and keeps your winning advantage. Several quiet moves were just as good, so this is fine.
Your bishop on f4 was attacked by the h5 knight, so it had to move, and Bg5 is fine. Be3 was very slightly better because on g5 the bishop can be chased with ...f6, but the difference is small.
